content.title: About
content.content: Cashews are the kidney-shaped seeds of the cashew tree (Anacardium occidentale), native to northeastern Brazil and now grown in tropical regions around the world. The nut hangs below a fleshy cashew apple and has a creamy, buttery, mildly sweet flavor. Cashews are eaten as a snack and used in stir-fries, curries, sauces, desserts, and plant-based dairy alternatives.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The cashew nut grows outside the cashew apple, a fruit that is also edible but highly perishable.
Cashews are related to mangoes, pistachios, and poison ivy.
The shell contains a caustic oil that can irritate skin, so cashews are always sold shelled and processed.
Cashews are used to make creamy plant-based sauces, cheeses, and milks.
Major cashew producers include Vietnam, India, and countries in West Africa.

items.title: Provides healthy fats
items.content: Cashews contain mostly unsaturated fats, which can be part of a heart-friendly diet.

items.title: Provides magnesium and copper
items.content: These minerals support muscle, nerve, and metabolic function.

items.title: Provides zinc and manganese
items.content: These support immune function and normal metabolism.

items.title: Provides protein
items.content: Cashews provide plant protein, which supports fullness.

items.title: Contains vitamin K and antioxidants
items.content: Cashews provide vitamin K and plant compounds with antioxidant properties.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: Cashew allergy is among the more common tree nut allergies and can be severe. People allergic to cashews may also react to pistachios.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: Cashews are calorie-dense, so portions should be moderate.

items.title: Added salt
items.content: Roasted and salted cashews can contain a lot of sodium.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Cashews contain oxalates, which people prone to kidney stones may need to limit.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cashews can be eaten as a snack, added to stir-fries, curries, salads, granola, and baked goods, or blended into creamy sauces, dips, desserts, and plant-based milks. Soaking cashews softens them for blending. Choose unsalted cashews when possible.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cashews in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place, or in the refrigerator or freezer for longer storage, since their oils can turn rancid. Discard cashews that smell sharp or taste bitter.
